notes:
I couldn't finish every verse. My page reads were cut off before verse 49 on both the full Enduring Word and Pulpit Commentary pages, so most of what follows comes from the search-result text for those and other pages. **Verses 53, 56–57 and 59 have no separate notes, and there's little on 63–64 and 69–70.** I found nothing from the Lutheran, Pentecostal, Catholic or Orthodox sites, bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org for these verses, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 49**
- Matthew Henry: Jesus would put up with anything rather than that the least jot or tittle of the word of God should fall to the ground. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_014.cfm
- Guzik (Enduring Word): Jesus marveled that they sent a small army to arrest Him. Yet, He was in command; with a word He could destroy all those who came to arrest Him. But Jesus went along in order to fulfill Scripture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Light of Israel Commentary: "I was with you" suggests some of the people who came out to arrest him were the very same people who were present when he was teaching in the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-51.html

**v. 50**
- Precept Austin points to the word "all": both Jesus' recent prediction and Zechariah's prophecy about the scattered sheep came true exactly. Jesus' prophecy less than a few hours old and Zechariah's prophecy some 500+ years old were both fulfilled to the letter! https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**vv. 51–52 (the young man)**
- Who he was is a long-running question:
  - Pulpit Commentary says there is good reason for supposing that he here describes what happened to himself, meaning Mark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-51.htm
  - Spurgeon also leaned towards Mark. He admits it is merely a supposition, but notes that Mark is the most impulsive of the Gospels. https://biblehub.com/sermons/mark/14-51.htm
  - Ellicott says the only reason to think of Mark is that Mark alone tells the story. He suggests Lazarus instead, guessing the linen sheet could have been Lazarus's old burial cloth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-51.htm
  - Barnes says he was clearly not one of the apostles, and may have been the owner of the garden. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/mark/14-51.html
  - GotQuestions thinks John Mark is the likeliest. https://www.gotquestions.org/Mark-fled-naked.html
- What the linen means:
  - Gill: probably a nightshirt or sheet grabbed in a hurry. He takes "the young men" who grabbed him to be Roman soldiers, who thought he was a disciple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-51.html
  - Constable: the word for "young man" means someone roughly 24–40, and the linen was a fairly costly outer garment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-51.html
- Why Mark tells it:
  - Matthew Henry: it shows how rough the arresting crowd was, and how narrowly the disciples escaped. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-51.html
  - Desiring God: don't build on guesses about his identity or symbolism. He is a concrete, vivid example of the terror they all felt and the completeness with which the Scriptures were fulfilled. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/a-mysterious-naked-guy-in-gethsemane-and-a-lesson-in-bible-interpretation

**v. 54**
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon notes that many have seen Peter's following "afar off" and "warming himself" as symbolical of his spiritual position with regard to his Master. https://biblehub.com/sermons/mark/14-62.htm
- Guzik: Peter sitting with the servants who beat Jesus shows that distance from Jesus makes us vulnerable when temptation arrives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 55**
- Precept Austin calls it a "kangaroo court". The Greek tense shows they kept looking for evidence again and again and found none. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Guzik: by Jewish law the trial was terribly illegal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 58**
- Guzik: in John 2:19 Jesus was talking about the temple of His body. He never said the "made with hands" words. The accusers were effectively painting Him as a terrorist out to destroy the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**vv. 60–61**
- Guzik: Jesus' silence fulfils Isaiah 53:7. Though He seemed to lose, He really won. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- A writer Guzik quotes says the high priest's question was a tacit confession that Christ had been proved innocent up till then. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Ligonier: "the Blessed One" stood in for God's name, probably because Jews avoided saying it aloud. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/son-man-right-hand-power
- Precept Austin: Matthew's account shows the high priest put Jesus under oath to try to make Him incriminate Himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 62**
- Precept Austin: "I am" is the Greek *ego eimi*, used in the Greek Old Testament at Exodus 3:14. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Ligonier:
  - Jesus answered with His own polite stand-in for God's name, "Power", while still claiming to be Messiah and Son of God.
  - "Son of Man" goes back mainly to Daniel 7:13–14.

  https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/son-man-right-hand-power
- Constable: Jesus was claiming to be the Judge of the men judging Him, and knew this confession would seal His conviction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-62.html
- Swete (quoted by Precept Austin): the words were also a final but ineffectual summons to repentance and faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Why was it called blasphemy? A writer Precept Austin quotes says claiming to be Messiah was not blasphemy in itself. The blasphemy lay in the language that seemed to claim glory belonging only to God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 63**
- Matthew Henry: some think the clothes the high priest tore were his official robes, worn for the occasion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_014.cfm

**v. 65**
- Chuck Smith: the spitting fulfilled a prophecy of Isaiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-62.html

**vv. 66–68**
- Matthew Henry: While the chief priests were abusing the Master, the servants were abusing the disciples. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_014.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: every word of Peter's denial is emphatic, as if he knew nothing about Jesus at all. It holds that all the denials took place in Caiaphas's house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/14.htm
- Ligonier: verse 68 uses two different Greek words for knowing, one for head-knowledge and one for personal knowledge. Peter denied both. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/roosters-crow

**vv. 70–71**
- Guzik: the bystanders recognised Peter as a Galilean by his speech. He then began to curse and swear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 72**
- On the two crowings:
  - Constable: only Mark mentions a second crowing. Peter remembered too little and too late. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-72.html
  - GotQuestions: Peter probably didn't notice the first crow, and Mark doesn't contradict the other Gospels. https://www.gotquestions.org/rooster-crowing-Peter.html
- On Peter's weeping:
  - Pulpit Commentary: the verb means long, continued weeping. https://biblehub.com/mark/14-72.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: Not with the remorse of Judas, but the godly sorrow of true repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-72.htm
  - Guzik, quoting another writer: it was remembering Christ's words that convicted Peter, not the rooster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

These are differences in emphasis rather than sharp disputes.
- **v. 62, when is the "coming with the clouds"?**
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) leaves it open: either at the destruction of Jerusalem, or at the last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-62.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian) says it means the final judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-62.html
  - The Berean Study Bible notes read it as His visible bodily return. https://biblehub.com/mark/14-62.htm
- **v. 72, what Peter's weeping shows**
  - Ligonier (Reformed) cites the view that true repentance is always God's gift by the Holy Spirit. It quotes Spurgeon that the Spirit usually works through means, here Peter's memory. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/roosters-crow
  - Wesley (Methodist) reads the verb as "he covered his head", a mourners' custom showing grief and shame. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-72.html

## 3. Other views

- **Early-church readings:**
  - Theophylact, an Orthodox Church Father, cited by the Expositor's Greek Testament, also took verse 72 to mean Peter covered his head to weep freely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-72.htm
  - A tradition traced to Clement says that for the rest of his life Peter knelt and wept whenever he heard a rooster crow. https://biblehub.com/sermons/mark/14-72.htm
- **Catholic:** catholic.com has an article on the young man of verses 51–52. The excerpt I saw argues against the "underdressed sleeper" idea, since people sometimes wore just one garment. I didn't see the author's own conclusion. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/another-theory-for-that-naked-man-in-mark
- **Popular speculation:** a Bible Hub Q&A page mentions a theory that the young man had just been baptised and wore baptismal linen. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_the_young_man_in_Mark_14_51_key.htm
